PROVENANCE CORRECTION (2026-08-31): the epic's original design cited drifted CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md as the motivating real defect. That motivation is withdrawn. Both files came from commit 4d81b55 'bd init', are byte-identical to it, and were never hand-edited; their difference is bd template-version skew between two recipe installs, not policy drift. 'bd setup claude --check' currently reports CLAUDE.md as stale and offers to regenerate it.

The architecture survives; its motivating example was wrong. A THIRD ownership class is added:
  CANONICAL - authored by us (README.md, BASELINE.md; no policy content exists yet)
  VENDOR    - owned by another tool's installer (everything bd setup emits)
  PROJECTED - derived by bin/ms from canonical
The substrate must not fight vendor installers for files they own. This makes the projector's refusal path load-bearing rather than theoretical.

title: Acceptance test: prove the substrate works and the boundary holds
description:
Why: one test is the whole point of v0.01. If it passes, the substrate is real; if it cannot be written, the design was wrong.

What: tests/acceptance.sh — one script, one pass/fail, three assertions.

LIVENESS
  Delete state/hostwatch/latest.json, then: systemctl --user start machine-state-hostwatch.service
  Within 30s latest.json exists again, parses as JSON, has schema==1, and collected_at is within 60s of now.

CONFINEMENT (write boundary)
  Run the same unit with an override whose ExecStart attempts a write to $HOME/ms-boundary-probe.
  The write MUST fail (EROFS/EACCES) and the file must not exist afterwards.

CONFINEMENT (network boundary)
  Run the same unit with an override whose ExecStart attempts socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM).
  It MUST fail with EAFNOSUPPORT/EPERM. No DNS, no connect, nothing that needs a live network to decide.

The test cleans up its own overrides. It asserts the sandbox denies things, not merely that the happy path works — a substrate whose boundary is untested is a boundary that does not exist.
design:
Both confinement probes run through the real unit via systemd drop-in overrides, so the test exercises the shipped sandbox rather than a re-declaration of it. Probes are inline python -c one-liners; no probe scripts to leave lying around.

The test must not require network, root, or an external service, so it stays runnable on a plane.
acceptance_criteria:
- tests/acceptance.sh exits 0 on this machine after bin/ms-agent install, and prints one line per assertion.
- Deliberately breaking the sandbox (removing RestrictAddressFamilies) makes the test fail — verified once during implementation and recorded in bead notes.
- The test leaves no drop-in overrides, probe files, or altered unit state behind.
- Result of the first passing run is recorded in the epic before closing it.

title: Write hostwatch collector (agents/hostwatch/run.py)
description:
Why: the resident payload. Deterministic stand-in for a future agent brain; proves the write path and the sandbox without needing an LLM.

What: single-file Python 3.14 stdlib script, no imports outside the stdlib, no argparse ceremony.

Collects a deliberately tiny read-only fact set:
- timestamp (UTC, ISO-8601), hostname, kernel release
- uptime seconds (/proc/uptime)
- load average (os.getloadavg)
- memory total/available (/proc/meminfo)
- root filesystem free bytes (os.statvfs on /)
- battery percent + AC state if /sys/class/power_supply exists, else null

Writes state/hostwatch/latest.json atomically (write temp in the same dir, os.replace). Repo root resolved from the script's own path, not from cwd or an env var.

On any collection error: still write a valid document with the failing field null and an 'errors' list. The agent must never leave a half-written or missing state file.
design:
Atomic replace matters because a human or a future reader may read latest.json at any moment, including mid-run. Same-directory temp keeps the rename on one filesystem (btrfs subvolume @home).

Schema is versioned from day one: top-level 'schema': 1. Cheap now, unavoidable later.

- python3 agents/hostwatch/run.py writes a valid JSON document to state/hostwatch/latest.json.
- Document contains schema, collected_at, and every field above; missing sources yield null plus an entry in errors, never a crash.

title: Write hardened systemd --user unit and timer
description:
Why: the sandbox IS the trust boundary. The unit file is where the permission model is actually enforced, rather than merely described.

What: systemd/machine-state-hostwatch.service (Type=oneshot) and .timer.

Service sandbox, at minimum:
  NoNewPrivileges=yes
  PrivateTmp=yes
  ProtectSystem=strict
  ProtectHome=read-only
  ReadWritePaths=/home/klaas/src/machine-state/state
  ProtectKernelTunables=yes
  ProtectControlGroups=yes
  RestrictSUIDSGID=yes
  RestrictNamespaces=yes
  LockPersonality=yes
  MemoryDenyWriteExecute=yes
  SystemCallFilter=@system-service
  RestrictAddressFamilies=AF_UNIX
  UMask=0077

Timer: OnStartupSec plus OnUnitActiveSec (15min), Persistent=false. No linger, so it only ticks inside a live session.
design:
RestrictAddressFamilies=AF_UNIX is chosen over IPAddressDeny for the network boundary: it is seccomp-enforced and therefore reliable in a --user unit, whereas IPAddressDeny needs BPF cgroup delegation that user scope may not have. It also fails loudly and testably (socket(AF_INET) raises), which the acceptance test depends on.

VERIFY during implementation: that ReadWritePaths= does in fact re-open the state dir read-write underneath ProtectHome=read-only in systemd 261. If it does not, drop ProtectHome and rely on ProtectSystem=strict plus ReadWritePaths, and record the change in SUBSTRATE.md.

Also verify @system-service does not block the atomic-replace path or /proc reads.

- systemd-analyze verify passes on both units.
- systemd-analyze security scores the service and the exposure level is recorded in the bead notes.
- Timer schedule is 15 minutes, non-persistent, no linger required.
- Unit references the repo paths only; no ExecStart outside the repo.

title: Resident-agent substrate v0.01
description:
Goal: the smallest end-to-end loop that proves a resident agent can live on this workstation — scheduled by the user session, sandboxed, observing read-only, and reporting into this repo. Not a distro, not a framework, not an agent runtime.

v0.01 proves the PLUMBING, not the reasoning. The resident payload is a deterministic stdlib-Python collector standing in for a future agent brain; swapping in an LLM is a later version. If the substrate is right, that swap touches one file.

Shape: one agent (hostwatch) + one systemd --user timer + one sandbox profile + one state file + one acceptance test.
design:
Constraints from BASELINE.md and live probes:
- systemd 261, +SECCOMP +BPF_FRAMEWORK; user manager present; Linger=no (agent lives only inside the login session — deliberate for v0.01).
- Python 3.14.7 stdlib only. No node/go/rust/docker, no pip, no venv, no AUR packages.

- Repo is at /home/klaas/src/machine-state; conservative git profile (no agent-initiated commits).

title: Write SUBSTRATE.md — the canonical/adapter contract
description:
Why: the substrate is a set of conventions. If they are not written in one place, every future agent, adapter, and managed config re-invents them. This document is the contract the projector and every adapter implement against.

What: SUBSTRATE.md at repo root, roughly two screens, stating concrete choices:

1. CANONICAL — the repo is the source of truth. canonical/ holds agent-neutral content: policy/ (operating rules), skills/ (neutral SKILL.md trees). desktop/ is reserved for Hyprland and Noctalia, empty in v0.01.
2. ADAPTERS — adapters/<agent>.toml declares that agent's targets. An adapter is a manifest, never content. Adding an agent = adding a manifest.
3. PROJECTION — exactly two mechanisms, render and link. One-way, canonical to target. Targets are derived artifacts: regenerable, removable, never hand-edited.
4. DRIFT — every projection is recorded in state/projection.json with source and target hashes. A hand-edit is a detectable, reportable condition, not a merge.
5. PROMOTION — the reverse path (target edit back into canonical) is deliberately manual and human-initiated. The substrate never guesses that a hand-edit was intentional.
6. BOUNDARY — what the projector may touch, and what requires a human.
7. NON-GOALS — the deferred list for v0.01.

Definition-only bead: no canonical/, no adapters/, no bin/ms.
design:
This doc supersedes the ad-hoc convention currently implied by the repo (two hand-mirrored instruction files, an .agents/ tree, and a .claude/ dir with no stated relationship between them). It should name that existing arrangement and say which parts become canonical and which become projections.

Write it so a future agent that has never seen this conversation can rebuild the substrate from the document alone.
acceptance_criteria:
- SUBSTRATE.md exists at repo root and covers all seven sections.
- Each section states one concrete choice with a one-line reason, not a survey of options.
- Explicitly resolves the status of the existing CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, .agents/, .claude/ and .codex/ paths: which becomes canonical, which becomes a projection.
- NON-GOALS includes at minimum: no reverse auto-sync, no agent-initiated git, no root or sudo, no network, no package installs, no desktop config in v0.01, no multi-machine.
- No directories or code created by this bead.
notes:
Rewritten twice: first from an open-ended 'where should things live' bead, then from the hostwatch framing. Now scoped to the canonical/adapter architecture.

DELIVERED 2026-08-31: SUBSTRATE.md, 206 lines, 9 sections.

DEVIATION FROM ACCEPTANCE: the bead specified seven sections and 'roughly two screens'. Shipped nine sections and roughly four. title: Experience cohesion: plan as a sibling epic once bru proves the vocabulary
description:
Placeholder holding a design review's conclusion so it is not lost. NOT yet an epic, deliberately.

THE GAP: machine-state governs state and machine-state-bru will govern runtime action, but neither
gives the workstation one vocabulary. Today a key could run a shell command, a Noctalia menu could
carry a third name for the same operation, and a shortcut preview could document a binding that no
longer exists — all working independently while the system as a whole misinforms its user.

THE PROPOSED LAYER: one semantic theme from which application themes derive; one keybinding
registry from which both live bindings and their preview derive; one action vocabulary shared by
keys, menus, agents, notifications and events; one application-role registry so workflows target
mail rather than proton-mail; and one account of which bindings are ours, a vendor's, or in
conflict — the binding equivalent of CANONICAL, VENDOR and PROJECTED.

THE SEAM: a stable namespaced action identifier. A key binding, a menu entry, an agent call and an
event binding all name desktop.application.open. The experience layer decides where an action
appears; the broker decides whether and how it may run. Neither assumes the other's authority.

WHY IT IS A SIBLING AND NOT A PHASE: cohesion spans durable state and runtime action; the broker is
deliberately runtime-only. Its declarations are canonical state projected by ms; it references
capability names but owns none.

WHY NOT YET, three reasons, all grounded:
  1. It would be planned against capability identifiers that do not exist until bru phases 1 and 2.
  2. Theme work is blocked behind machine-state-a22. Noctalia already owns cross-application
     theming here — 54 templates, live theme files in six applications — and projecting a canonical
     theme into them would start a rewrite war over settings nobody here has an opinion about.
  3. binds.lua declares 75 bindings and is byte-identical to the CachyOS template. Zero are ours.
     A keybinding registry would begin by describing vendor state, not owning it, which is a more
     modest and more honest claim than generating a keymap.

The full review is machine-state-bru.md at repository root.
acceptance_criteria:
- Opened as an epic only after bru phases 1 and 2 are complete and machine-state-a22 is decided.
- The first vertical slice is deliberately small: one token set, two targets, one binding, one preview, one role.
- Key bindings and event bindings keep distinct schemas and loaders.

Emitted at the point of action, structured, rather than harvested from logs afterwards.

This is what dcg history cannot give: it records shell commands and whether they were allowed, with no intent, no outcome, and a session_id unique per invocation. Emitting at source is how this machine gets an analysable corpus without acquiring an orchestrator.

A partial record is worse than none for analysis, so this precedes events rather than following them: an event stream whose invocations are unrecorded produces a biased corpus that looks complete from inside.

title: Phase 4: Event sources and bindings
description:
Typed events with provenance, bound to catalogue entries.

Eight sources verified present in CAPABILITIES.md section 2; Hyprland's socket was read with the stdlib alone. A timer is just another event, so scheduling needs no scheduler.

Bindings are declared, never discovered. Nothing runs because it was dropped in a directory. Still supervised at this phase: report class only.

title: Phase 5: Unattended operation
description:
Grants become live and consequence classes are enforced at invocation.

Deliberately last. Grants govern nothing until there are capabilities to govern, and the grants schema was designed against zero capabilities so it should be expected to need revision once a real one exists.

title: Test whether /etc/codex/managed_config.toml can carry a dcg hook
description:
Codex is installed and UNGUARDED; ms status exits non-zero on it. The blocker was recorded as: bd setup codex owns both hooks files Codex reads, and JSON offers no marker for co-ownership.

There may be a third path. The Codex binary references /etc/codex/config.toml, /etc/codex/requirements.toml and /etc/codex/managed_config.toml, plus keys managed_config, managed_features, managed_dir and managed_allowed_domains_only. A managed config path would be root-owned — outside bd's ownership AND outside agent reach, which fits the grants boundary exactly rather than working around it.

TWO THINGS DECIDE IT, neither answerable from the binary:
  1. can managed_config carry hooks at all
  2. does it OVERRIDE user config, or is it overridden

Point 2 matters because dcg's equivalent layer fails precisely here: its system config is the
LOWEST priority, so a user-writable file overrides it. If Codex's managed layer is also low
priority it is useless for this. Enterprise managed config is usually highest priority, but that is
an expectation, not a finding.

Deliberately not answered by more strings-spelunking. That approach already produced two wrong
conclusions in this project — grepping Noctalia's config for 'include' instead of reading its help,
and inferring Codex's SessionStart behaviour from a directory's absence.

TEST: a probe file is written to scratchpad. Installing it needs sudo, which is the boundary
working as intended. Then check whether codex doctor reports it loaded, and whether a hook fires.
acceptance_criteria:
- Established empirically whether managed_config is read, whether it carries hooks, and its precedence relative to user config.
- If it works: dcg is wired for Codex from a root-owned path and ms status stops reporting UNGUARDED.
- If it does not: the finding is recorded in canonical/tooling/codex.md and one of the other three routes is chosen.

title: Decide Noctalia's status before designing a theme protocol
description:
An external architecture review proposed consuming Omarchy themes as an upstream: a semantic palette, adapters per application, and a trust filter that strips executable content from third-party theme repositories. The trust filter in particular is sound and matches this repository's rule that bindings are declared, never discovered.

But the review could not know what is already here. Noctalia IS a cross-application theming engine on this machine: 54 templates in ~/.local/state/noctalia/community-templates/, most carrying an executable apply.sh, six of them live — writing into alacritty, kitty, btop, gtk-3.0, gtk-4.0 and qt6ct. See canonical/tooling/noctalia.md.

So the question here is not how to consume Omarchy themes. It is: Noctalia already owns cross-application theming, so do we displace it, wrap it, or leave it? Adopting those files into canonical would start a rewrite war with a theming engine, over settings we have no opinion about.

Worth noting the convergence: Noctalia's template model is the theme-as-protocol idea, already implemented and running. The cheapest outcome may be to record it as the theme provider and build nothing.
acceptance_criteria:
- A decision recorded: displace, wrap, or leave Noctalia's theming.
- Any theme protocol design comes after that decision, not before.
- If a third-party theme source is ever consumed, executable content is stripped.
notes:
LIKELY ANSWERED, 2026-09-02, by grounding rather than design. Noctalia already IS the semantic
theme registry this repository was considering building:

  config.toml declares builtin_ids = btop, gtk3, gtk4, kcolorscheme, kitty, qt, alacritty
  wallpaper_scheme = m3-tonal-spot, a semantic scheme rather than a copied palette
  54 community templates act as per-application adapters
  noctalia msg exposes color-scheme-get/set and theme-mode-get/set/toggle at runtime
  six applications have live theme files written by it

That is one semantic source, a declared target list, adapters, and runtime control — the exact
architecture a canonical theme layer would have provided. Building one would reimplement a working
system in order to own it, and would start a rewrite war across six applications over settings
nobody here has an opinion about.

PROPOSED DECISION: leave it. Noctalia is the theme provider. Our contribution is to record it,
which canonical/tooling/noctalia.md already does, and to expose its runtime commands as
capabilities once the capability layer exists — cohesion by reference rather than replacement.

This removes theme work from the agent-first version one entirely.

title: Explore Omarchy patterns for the agent-native workstation
description:
PURPOSE

Preserve architectural ideas from Omarchy that may inform machine-state without copying Omarchy by rote. This bead is for later elaboration and design work only. It does not authorize implementation, package installation, desktop mutation, or expansion of the current substrate boundary.

CONTEXT

machine-state aims to make resident agents policy-governed operators of the CachyOS workstation and user session, rather than merely applications launched inside the desktop. Omarchy solves a different problem, but several aspects of its interaction design are relevant.

PATTERNS WORTH EXPLORING

1. One capability, several interfaces: the same operation should be reachable through an agent tool or API, a CLI, a Noctalia menu or panel, and optionally a Hyprland binding. Human and agent automation should not become separate systems.

2. A unified, discoverable control vocabulary: provide self-describing commands, structured JSON discovery, schemas, completion, and help so agents can inspect available operations rather than memorize them.

3. Human and machine discoverability: pair a searchable human capability menu with a machine-readable catalogue containing availability, inputs, effects, risk class, and authorization requirements.

4. Structured event hooks: consider events such as window.opened, notification.received, mail.received, meeting.starting, battery.low, network.changed, process.crashed, user.idle, and agent.action.completed. Prefer typed event data and provenance over blindly executing scripts from directories.

5. Event-to-agent workflows: examples include crash diagnosis from coredumps, mail classification and proposed triage, workspace layouts when a monitor connects, process analysis on low battery, and contextual actions derived from notifications. Agents should receive structured OS context rather than infer state from screenshots.

6. Explicit extension contracts: capability packages could use namespaced manifests declaring operations, dependencies, credentials, services, exposed data, audit behavior, and consequence or approval class. Their implementation might be MCP, a local service, or a CLI without changing the policy model.

7. Opinionated defaults with narrow override seams: retain the machine-state rule to own the smallest addressable region while making supported customization paths obvious.

8. Transactional change and recovery: preview effects, capture before-state, apply atomically, validate afterward, retain rollback, and record provenance.

9. Selective supporting ideas: semantic themes shared across applications; logical default-app roles; actionable notifications; and a control-plane panel showing agents, approvals, recent actions, guard status, and automation failures.

IDEAS NOT TO INHERIT

- Auto-approved or unattended agents as the normal safety model.
- Wholesale ownership of user or vendor configuration.
- A monolithic desktop shell as the architecture.
- Unsandboxed plugins as the default extension mechanism.
- Full configuration reinstall as routine recovery.
- Package and application curation as the center of machine-state.

ARCHITECTURAL CONSTRAINT

Do not turn bin/ms into the runtime control plane. ms should remain content-agnostic and responsible for canonical projection and drift. If the idea matures, explore a separate peer substrate tool or capability broker, recorded under canonical/tooling, that exposes governed runtime operations shared by humans and agents.

PRIMARY SOURCES CONSULTED

- https://omarchy.org/manual/omarchy-cli/
- https://omarchy.org/manual/hotkeys/
- https://omarchy.org/manual/toggles-idle-screensaver/
- https://omarchy.org/manual/dotfiles/
- https://omarchy.org/manual/shell-plugins/
- https://omarchy.org/manual/updates/
- https://omarchy.org/manual/ai/
- https://omarchy.org/manual/making-your-own-theme/

STATUS

Exploration backlog. Elaborate the capability model, authority boundaries, event semantics, and relationship to Noctalia or Hyprland before proposing implementation.
acceptance_criteria:
- The exploration distinguishes transferable design principles from Omarchy-specific implementation choices.
- A later design pass defines the capability model, event model, authority classes, and human or agent interfaces.
- The relationship between the proposed runtime layer, ms, Noctalia, Hyprland, MCP, and local services is documented.
- Security, credential handling, auditability, reversibility, and plugin isolation are addressed before implementation work is proposed.
- No implementation is performed as part of this bead without the issue being explicitly refined or superseded by implementation issues.

comments.author: root-mechanicum
comments.text:
SCOPE DECIDED 2026-09-01, after discussing this bead against the dispatch/Gluon approach.

Item 4, structured event hooks, is the chosen direction, and it turns out to answer three open
problems at once rather than one:

  triggering  - the event is the trigger, so no admission control is needed
  authority   - a declared consequence class per capability (items 3 and 6) replaces "ask first",
                which cannot survive unattended operation because it needs someone to answer
  provenance  - agent.action.completed as a typed event emits the record at source, instead of
                harvesting it from logs afterwards

BOUNDARY, now written into SUBSTRATE.md Purpose and non-goals. machine-state covers REACTIVE and
SCHEDULED operation only. A timer is just another event, so one model covers both. It explicitly
does NOT cover sustained autonomous work — an agent turned loose on a backlog for hours. That is a
real thing to want and a different problem: it needs admission control, scope freezing, budgets,
and an answer for what an agent's death means. It belongs on a machine dedicated to it.

This matters because the failure modes that dominate sustained autonomy do not arise here at all.
The dispatch test suite names them plainly — nodeltafloor, unpushedexit, salvage, stalemarker,
pausefreeze — and every one is a property of a long-lived agent. Conflating the two models would
import all of that machinery to solve problems this machine does not have.

The bead's own IDEAS NOT TO INHERIT line, rejecting auto-approved unattended agents as the normal
safety model, is upheld rather than overridden: unattended is not the same as auto-approved. What
makes an event-triggered capability safe is that its consequence class was declared before it ran.

The ARCHITECTURAL CONSTRAINT in this bead is also confirmed independently. A separate peer tool or
capability broker, recorded under canonical/tooling and never folded into bin/ms, is the same
relationship machine-state already has with dcg: record it, verify it, do not own it. The reason is
the same too — the substrate must not hold authority over a layer that governs it, because
canonical is agent-writable by design.

NEXT: the design pass this bead asks for. Capability model, event semantics, consequence classes,
and the relationship to Noctalia and Hyprland as event sources.

comments.author: root-mechanicum
comments.text:
DESIGN PASS DONE 2026-09-01. Written to CAPABILITIES.md at repo root, 206 lines. Status is design;
nothing implemented.

Grounded first rather than designed first. Every event class this bead names has a verified source
on this machine: Hyprland .socket2.sock (read with nothing but Python's socket module, 40 typed
events in nine seconds), org.freedesktop.Notifications, UPower with BAT0, NetworkManager, login1,
systemd1, dev.noctalia.Mpris, and systemd user timers. No new runtime is needed, which matters on a
box with no node, go or rust.

WHAT THE DESIGN SETTLES

A timer is an event. time.daily differs from mail.received only in what produced it, so scheduling
needs no scheduler and one model covers both. That is the largest simplification available.

Consequence classes replace free/ask-first/never, which cannot survive unattended operation because
asking needs an answerer. Four classes decided by reversibility and whether the effect leaves the
machine: observe changes nothing and always runs; report adds a record a human reads and always
runs; adjust touches reversible session state and runs only where a binding grants it; commit is
durable or outward and never runs unattended, it raises for a human as a bead.

Provenance is emitted, not harvested. Every invocation emits agent.action.completed carrying
binding, capability, class, inputs, outcome, duration and actor. That is what dcg history cannot
give: it records shell commands and whether they were allowed, with no intent, no outcome, and a
session_id unique per invocation rather than per session. Emitting at the point of action is how
this machine gets a corpus without acquiring an orchestrator.

THE OPEN QUESTION THAT MATTERS MOST

Where do grants live so agents cannot widen them. canonical/ is agent-writable by design — that is
the point of ms project — so capability manifests may be agent-writable, declaring what a
capability IS, while the grants deciding which bindings may run unattended must sit outside agent
reach. Information may flow up from canonical; authority may never. Same rule that keeps
dcg's config unprojected. The mechanism is unresolved: a root-owned file, or dcg's
enforcement-only pattern where a file can tighten but never loosen, which is the one shape provably
safe to hand an agent. Everything else in the design rests on this.

Four further open questions are recorded in section 8: whether the broker must be resident and what
that implies given Linger=no; what the first capability should be; whether Noctalia can be
subscribed to or only dispatched to; and how capabilities reach a human, probably beads by class.

The bead's ARCHITECTURAL CONSTRAINT is honoured throughout — the broker is a peer to bin/ms,
recorded under canonical/tooling when it exists, never folded in.

title: Phase 2: bring Noctalia under canonical/desktop
description:
Deferred deliberately when Hyprland was projected on 2026-09-01. Noctalia is a harder case and should not be forced into Hyprland's shape.

WHY IT IS DIFFERENT:
- Single ~/.config/noctalia/config.toml, no include or drop-in mechanism found. Hyprland's require() chain is what made the clean 'our own module, loaded last' design possible; Noctalia has no equivalent.
- TOML makes duplicate keys an ERROR, so splice cannot override a value the way a later Lua call can. Owning a marker region in that file would not let us change a setting.
- The config is very likely APP-WRITTEN: 58 machine-formatted setting lines, and Noctalia is a GUI shell with a settings panel. If it rewrites config.toml when a setting changes, canonicalizing it makes every UI tweak drift, and ms project would overwrite the user's changes. That is the bd problem with no marker escape hatch.
- Not package-owned (pacman owns /usr/bin/noctalia at 5.0.0_beta.10-1.1, but not the config).

FIRST QUESTION, before any design: does Noctalia rewrite its own config.toml? Change a setting in its UI and watch the file. If it does, the honest answer may be that it is not canonicalizable yet, and the record should say so — like the Codex wiring gap.

'noctalia config' has validate and replay helpers worth investigating; a validate command would make a good tooling-record check regardless of whether the file becomes managed.
acceptance_criteria:
- Established empirically whether Noctalia rewrites config.toml.
- Either a design that survives that answer, or a recorded decision that it is not canonicalizable yet, with the reason.
- canonical/tooling/noctalia.md exists either way.
notes:
INVESTIGATED 2026-09-01. Four of the assumptions in this bead's description were wrong, and the corrections matter more than the conclusion.

WRONG: 'no include or drop-in mechanism'. There is one, and it is directory-based rather than an include directive: noctalia reads EVERY *.toml in the config dir and merges them. Found in 'noctalia config export --help', not by grepping the config for 'include' — which is how the wrong conclusion was reached.
WRONG: 'TOML forbids the duplicate keys an override would need'. True of a single file, irrelevant here: override happens at file level.
WRONG: 'the config is likely app-written'. config.toml is untouched since install. The app writes to a SEPARATE file, ~/.local/state/noctalia/settings.toml.
WRONG: an earlier claim in session that settings.toml did not exist. It does, dated 2026-08-30 15:18; it had been truncated out of an 'ls | head -10'.

ACTUAL ARCHITECTURE, a three-layer stack:
  base       ~/.config/noctalia/config.toml         VENDOR, byte-identical to /etc/skel
  drop-in    ~/.config/noctalia/*.toml              ours to use
  overrides  ~/.local/state/noctalia/settings.toml  VENDOR, app-written

Verified in an isolated XDG_CONFIG_HOME, never against the live shell: a drop-in is read; it MERGES rather than replaces (21 sections before and after); load order is alphabetical and LATER WINS — a file sorting before config.toml lost to it, so the filename is load-bearing.

SEAM: a pure render of ~/.config/noctalia/machine-state.toml. No splice, no marker, nothing of the vendor's touched — cleaner than Hyprland, which needed a spliced require line.

NOT PROJECTED, deliberately: there is nothing to project. config.toml is byte-identical to skel, and settings.toml holds only app-generated runtime state — a schema version, lock-screen widget geometry keyed to @eDP-1, and wallpaper bookkeeping. No Noctalia decision has been made on this machine. Projecting an empty file to claim coverage would be green-for-the-wrong-reason. The adapter is three lines the day there is a decision.

KNOWN LIMIT, recorded in the tooling record: we would own the declarative layer, not the effective value. The app's settings.toml overrides our drop-in, so a change made in the Noctalia UI silently wins over canonical and ms diff would NOT report it — our file is unchanged, only the effective value differs. Same shape as dcg doctor verifying installation rather than posture. The fix, if it matters, is comparing 'noctalia config export merged' against canonical, not fighting the app for its own state file.

canonical/tooling/noctalia.md written, with a 'noctalia config validate' check proven falsifiable (exit 1, 'config invalid', on a broken config in an isolated dir).
close_reason: Investigated. Seam identified and proven (directory drop-in, render only); nothing projected because no Noctalia decision exists to capture. Tooling record written with a falsifiable check and the declarative-vs-effective limit recorded.

title: Your hypr config is a frozen copy of a package-maintained template
description:
~/.config/hypr was copied from /etc/skel/.config/hypr at account creation. That skel tree is owned by the package cachyos-hypr-noctalia (1.2.5-1 today) and moves with upgrades; your copy does not, and nothing reports the divergence.

They are identical today, verified 2026-09-01 — apart from canonical/desktop/hypr/machine-state.lua, which is ours. So this is not a problem yet. It becomes one silently, which is the same shape as the stale bd claude integration that sat unnoticed for a day until a tooling record turned it into a check.

Worth a check that compares ~/.config/hypr/config against /etc/skel/.config/hypr/config and reports files that have diverged, ignoring machine-state.lua. Now that the two decisions live in our own module and the template files are pristine, any difference at all is either a package update worth adopting or an unrecorded hand-edit — both things you want to see.

Not urgent. File it before it matters rather than discover it after.
acceptance_criteria:
- A check exists that reports divergence between ~/.config/hypr/config and the skel template.
- machine-state.lua is excluded from the comparison.
- Wired into a tooling record so ms status surfaces it, or explicitly deferred with a reason.
close_reason: Closed by the hypr tooling record: its check compares ~/.config/hypr/config against /etc/skel, excluding machine-state.lua, and is proven falsifiable. ms status now reports 'template pristine' or 'template diverged'.

title: Refresh the stale bd claude integration in CLAUDE.md
description:
ms status now surfaces this on every run: the claude harness reports 'integration stale'.

bd setup claude --check reports CLAUDE.md as installed but STALE. Its block carries template hash 6cd5cc61 while the current template is 970c3bf2 — the same skew found during the machine-state-9tw.2 provenance investigation, present since bd init on 2026-08-30 and never addressed. The only content difference is one line (bd dolt push) in the session-close snippet.

Fix: run 'bd setup claude' with the working directory inside the repo. It rewrites only bd's own marker block; the experiment in machine-state-9tw.2 confirmed all out-of-marker content survives, and machine-state-9tw.4 confirmed our MACHINE-STATE POLICY region survives it too.

VENDOR MAINTENANCE, not substrate work: this is invoking bd's own installer on a file bd owns. Kept separate from the v0.01 epic deliberately.

Note the -C trap: bd setup <recipe> --check ignores -C and inspects the real cwd, so cd into the repo rather than passing -C.
acceptance_criteria:
- bd setup claude --check reports CLAUDE.md as current.
- ms status shows the claude harness as integrated.
- Our MACHINE-STATE POLICY region, if projected by then, is intact afterwards.
notes:
DONE 2026-08-31. Ran 'bd setup claude' with cwd inside the repo. Output: 'Updated existing beads section in CLAUDE.md'.

The diff was exactly two lines, both inside bd's own marker block, and exactly what the machine-state-9tw.2 provenance investigation predicted:
  hash 6cd5cc61 -> 970c3bf2
  + 'bd dolt push' added to the session-close snippet

CO-TENANCY HELD ON THE LIVE FILE. Our MACHINE-STATE POLICY region survived bd's rewrite untouched, ms diff exits 0, and .claude/settings.json was not modified ('Hook already registered').

bd setup claude --check now reports CLAUDE.md as (current). ms status reports the claude harness as 'integrated'; state/tooling.json updated accordingly on the next status run.

This is the first time the two owners have written to the same live file in sequence, and it behaved exactly as the scratch experiment said it would.
close_reason: bd setup claude run; block refreshed to 970c3bf2, our region intact, ms diff clean, check reports current.

title: Decide the substantive agent operating policy for this machine
description:
Why: with machine-state-9tw.8 authoring only mechanical facts, this workstation still has no AUTHORED policy on how resident agents should behave. Today that guidance comes entirely from bd's vendor block (conservative git profile, task tracking rules, session close protocol) — text nobody here chose, inherited from an installer's default template.

That may be fine. But it should be a decision rather than an accident, and it is the user's to make, not the substrate's.

Questions, once there is appetite:
  a. Keep deferring to bd's block, or author our own operating rules in canonical/policy?
  b. If our own: which rules actually differ from bd's defaults for this machine?
  c. Does policy differ per harness, or is one neutral set correct?
  d. Shell hygiene: the rules bd ships name apt-get and brew, which are wrong here (apt-get is aliased to 'man pacman'; pacman is the real package manager, and no cp/mv/rm -i aliases exist). If we want correct guidance for this machine, it has to be ours.

Not in v0.01: the substrate must prove it can carry policy before there is any point arguing about the policy it carries.
acceptance_criteria:
- Each of (a)-(d) answered, or the whole thing consciously deferred again with a reason.
- Any rules adopted land in canonical/policy fragments and reach both harnesses through the existing manifests.
notes:
ANSWERED AND APPLIED 2026-09-01.

(a) Mostly defer to bd, plus one small fragment. bd's managed block covers task tracking, the three agent profiles, and session completion, and its conservative default is what this work actually ran under. None of it restated.

(b) Four rules, in canonical/policy/20-operating.md, each one something this work actually did rather than aspiration: this repo edits a live workstation, so draft-then-apply for anything outside it; experiments run in throwaway copies, never the live tree; never issue a command that can block on a prompt; a dcg refusal is answered by narrowing the command, never by disabling the guard.

(c) One neutral set. Harness differences already live in the harness fragments. Policy that varies per harness is exactly how CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md drifted apart originally. Verified after projecting: the rules are byte-identical in both files.

(d) Fixed, and more besides. Removed 45 lines of bd-init boilerplate from AGENTS.md: the Non-Interactive Shell Commands section (recommended apt-get -y and brew, on the false premise that cp/mv/rm carry -i aliases here), the architecture blockquote citing a .beads/dolt/ path that has never existed in this workspace and which bd's own current block contradicts 60 lines below it, and a duplicate Quick Reference. Verified in a scratch copy first that bd setup codex does NOT restore any of it — that prose was written once at bd init and never maintained.

HAND-EDIT TO A FILE WE DO NOT OWN, recorded deliberately: the deletions touch bytes outside our marker pair. The rule against that constrains the PROJECTOR; a deliberate, git-tracked, one-time correction of orphaned vendor prose is a different act. It should not become precedent — if it recurs, the ownership model erodes by habit.

OPEN CONCERN: our spliced region is now 47 lines in CLAUDE.md and 46 in AGENTS.md, up from 30, and is the largest single block in either file. AGENTS.md is net 45 lines shorter overall so the files are not worse off, but the guest-in-someone-else's-file principle from machine-state-9tw.8 is stretched. If the region grows again the fix is to move the bulk into the machine-state skill, which agents load on demand, and leave a pointer in the region.
close_reason: Operating policy authored, projected to both harnesses byte-identically, and 45 lines of stale bd-init boilerplate removed from AGENTS.md.

title: Write bin/ms-agent install/uninstall helper
description:
Why: installation is the one moment the substrate reaches outside the repo. It should be a single reviewable script, reversible, and user-scope only.

What: bin/ms-agent with three subcommands:
  install   - mkdir -p ~/.config/systemd/user, symlink the two units from systemd/, systemctl --user daemon-reload, enable --now the timer
  uninstall - disable --now the timer, remove the two symlinks, daemon-reload
  status    - systemctl --user status for both units plus the age of state/hostwatch/latest.json

Symlinks, not copies: the repo stays the single source of truth and an edit to a unit needs only daemon-reload.

Hard rules: no sudo anywhere in the script, no writes outside ~/.config/systemd/user, idempotent (running install twice is a no-op), and it refuses to run as root.
acceptance_criteria:
- install then uninstall then install leaves the same state; no duplicate or dangling symlinks.
- Script exits non-zero with a clear message if run as root or if systemctl --user is unavailable.
- Contains no sudo, no pacman, no writes outside ~/.config/systemd/user.
- uninstall leaves the machine with no trace of the agent outside the repo.
close_reason: Superseded by machine-state-9tw: hostwatch was a new monitoring program, not the substrate beneath existing agents.

title: EVAL: does the event model produce useful behaviour
description:
SHARED CONTEXT (true for every bead in this epic)

The tool is a PEER to bin/ms and must never be folded into it. ms governs durable projection and
drift; this governs runtime capabilities and actions. Folding them gives the projector a runtime
and the runtime the projector's write access. Read SUBSTRATE.md and CAPABILITIES.md in this
repository before starting; they are the contract, not background reading.

Constraints that apply throughout:
- Python 3.14 standard library only. No pip, no venv, no new runtime. This machine has no node,
  go or rust toolchain and is not to acquire one.
- Never root, never sudo, no network, no git invocation.
- dcg guards the shell beneath everything. A refusal is answered by narrowing the command, never
  by disabling the guard.
- Every check must be proven able to FAIL, not merely to pass. See SUBSTRATE.md section 5. A
  check that cannot fail reports green for the wrong reason; that has already happened twice in
  this repository.
- Task tracking is bd. Do not use markdown TODO lists. bd human is the escalation channel.
- Consequence classes are observe, report, adjust, commit. Defined in CAPABILITIES.md section 4.

The design claim is that reactive operation is genuinely useful, not merely possible. Test it.

METHOD: bind two or three real events to report-class capabilities and use the machine normally for
a period. Then assess:
- did the bindings fire when expected, and only then
- was the output useful or noise
- how many false triggers occurred
- did any binding fire in a way the person found surprising or unwelcome

WHAT FAILURE TEACHES: noise is the likeliest failure and it is fatal to the whole approach, because
a person who learns to ignore agent output has lost the benefit while keeping the cost. If
bindings are noisy, either the predicates are too loose or the event was the wrong trigger.
acceptance_criteria:
- At least two bindings run against real use for a recorded period.
- False trigger count recorded.
- A judgement recorded on whether the output was useful or noise, with reasoning.

title: Profiles: composable sets over adapters
description:
adapters/ is a flat list of target systems — claude, codex, hypr, git. There is no way to say 'this machine is base + laptop + development' and have that select a set.
